questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of recurrent major depressive episodes is enrolled in an imaging study. Volumetric MRI shows reduced hippocampal and prefrontal cortical volume with enlargement of the amygdala. She reports 6 years of unremitting occupational stress and caregiving strain. Genotyping reveals a Val66Met polymorphism. Which molecular change most directly links her chronic stress exposure to the observed structural findings?

answers.C: Decreased interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha
answers.D: Increased AMPA receptor trafficking to the synapse
answers.E: Increased hippocampal neurogenesis and synapse formation

explanations.A: Chronic stress and the Val66Met polymorphism both reduce BDNF, which normally promotes neuronal survival, dendritic growth, and neuroplasticity, producing atrophy and synapse loss in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.
explanations.B: Chronic stress raises rather than lowers extracellular glutamate, and the resulting excitotoxicity and oxidative stress contribute to the atrophy seen here.
explanations.C: Falling inflammatory cytokines would be protective; depression is characterized by elevated IL-1beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha that disrupt the blood-brain barrier and impair BDNF signaling.
explanations.D: Enhanced AMPA receptor subunit trafficking is a marker of intact neuroplasticity and is a proposed mechanism of rapid-acting antidepressants, not of stress-induced atrophy.
explanations.E: Increased neurogenesis would predict preserved or enlarged hippocampal volume; chronic stress instead decreases formation of new hippocampal neurons.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis develops 3 months of anhedonia, fatigue, hypersomnia, and psychomotor slowing. She has had no change in her medications and denies prior mood episodes. Her joint disease has flared, and serum IL-6 and C-reactive protein are markedly elevated. Which mechanism best explains the relationship between her systemic inflammatory state and her depressive symptoms?

answers.A: Blockade of monoamine oxidase A within presynaptic terminals
answers.B: Cytokine-driven shift of tryptophan toward neurotoxic metabolites
answers.D: Increased hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor signaling
answers.E: Selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra

explanations.A: Monoamine oxidase inhibition raises synaptic monoamines and is an antidepressant mechanism, not a consequence of systemic inflammation.
explanations.B: Elevated IL-1beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha disrupt the blood-brain barrier, activate microglia, and divert tryptophan metabolism toward neurotoxic kynurenine metabolites while impairing BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity.
explanations.C: Inflammation and chronic stress activate rather than suppress the CRH-ACTH-cortisol axis in depression.
explanations.D: Inflammatory cytokines impair BDNF signaling; increased BDNF would promote neuroplasticity and protect against depression.
explanations.E: Nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration produces Parkinson disease, a cause of secondary depression, but is not the mechanism of cytokine-associated mood symptoms.

questions.question: A health system has funding to place depression screening staff in a single outpatient setting and wants to reach the demographic group with the highest prevalence of major depressive episodes. Population data confirm that roughly 7.8% of U.S. adults have experienced at least one major depressive episode, and that a third of affected adults never receive treatment. Which group should be prioritized for screening?

explanations.A: Young adults do have the highest age-specific rates, but prevalence in men is consistently lower than in women across every age stratum.
explanations.B: Older men combine the lower-prevalence sex with a lower-prevalence age band, making this the least productive screening target.
explanations.C: Prevalence of major depressive episodes is highest in the 18-25 year age group and higher in women than men, so young adult women represent the peak-prevalence group.
explanations.D: Middle-aged women have substantial prevalence but lower rates than the 18-25 year peak.
explanations.E: Older women have lower prevalence of major depressive episodes than young adult women, though depression in this group is frequently underdiagnosed.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man reports feeling "low and gloomy" nearly every day for the past 3 years. He describes overeating, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and hopelessness. He has never gone longer than 3 weeks feeling like himself. He has never had a period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep, has never been hospitalized, and denies substance use. He works full time but finds it joyless. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

explanations.A: Bipolar II requires a hypomanic episode, which he has never experienced.
explanations.B: Cyclothymia requires alternating hypomanic and depressive periods; his course is uniformly depressed without elevated periods.
explanations.C: DMDD is diagnosed in children 6-10 years old with chronic irritability and temper outbursts, not in adults.
explanations.D: Depressed mood most days for at least 2 years with at least two additional symptoms and no symptom-free interval exceeding 2 months defines persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
explanations.E: PMDD requires symptoms confined to the luteal phase of most menstrual cycles, which does not apply to this patient.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is brought in for her fourth depressive episode in 3 years. Each episode has lasted about 3 weeks with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, and one episode with auditory hallucinations. Her mother was hospitalized for postpartum psychosis. Two weeks after starting sertraline last year she became irritable, talkative, and slept 3 hours nightly. Which underlying diagnosis best accounts for this course?

explanations.A: Onset before age 25, brief highly recurrent episodes, atypical features, psychosis, a family history of postpartum psychosis, and antidepressant-induced irritability with decreased sleep all point toward an underlying bipolar diathesis.
explanations.B: DMDD applies to chronically irritable children aged 6-10 years and cannot be diagnosed here.
explanations.C: A single-episode designation is impossible given four discrete episodes, and it would not explain the antidepressant-induced activation.
explanations.D: Persistent depressive disorder requires 2 years of nearly continuous depressed mood rather than brief recurrent episodes with intervening wellness.
explanations.E: Substance-induced depression would require temporal linkage to intoxication or withdrawal, which is absent.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman describes 1 year of recurrent mood swings, irritability, breast tenderness, bloating, and a sense of being overwhelmed. A prospective symptom diary shows that symptoms begin 5 to 7 days before menses in nearly every cycle, start improving within a few days of menstrual onset, and are absent in the week after menses. She has no symptoms during the follicular phase. Which diagnosis best fits?

answers.C: Major depressive disorder with anxious distress

explanations.A: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes not tied to the menstrual cycle.
explanations.B: Cyclothymia involves alternating hypomanic and depressive symptoms over 2 years, unrelated to menses.
explanations.C: MDD requires at least 2 weeks of continuous symptoms; her symptoms remit predictably with menstrual onset.
explanations.D: PDD requires at least 2 years of depressed mood most days with no symptom-free window over 2 months.
explanations.E: Affective lability, irritability, and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase of most cycles that remit shortly after menses onset define PMDD.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated for 14 months of daily irritable and angry mood present at home and at school. His parents describe severe temper outbursts four times per week that are grossly out of proportion to the trigger and inappropriate for his developmental level. Between outbursts he remains persistently angry rather than returning to baseline. He has never had a period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. Which diagnosis best fits?

explanations.A: Bipolar I requires a distinct manic episode with elevated or expansive mood and decreased need for sleep, which is absent.
explanations.B: Chronic non-episodic irritable mood most of the day nearly every day for 12 or more months with frequent developmentally inappropriate outbursts in more than one setting in a 6-10 year old defines DMDD.
explanations.C: MDD requires depressed mood or anhedonia with four or more additional neurovegetative symptoms, not chronic irritability with outbursts.
explanations.D: ODD features defiant and argumentative behavior but lacks the persistent angry or irritable mood between outbursts that defines DMDD.
explanations.E: In children PDD can present as irritability for 1 year, but it does not include the severe recurrent temper outbursts central to this presentation.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman reports 4 months of depressed mood, fatigue, 8-kg weight gain, hypersomnia, and impaired concentration. She has no prior psychiatric history and no family history of mood disorder. Examination shows dry skin, cold intolerance, a heart rate of 52/min, and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Laboratory studies are shown. Which diagnosis best explains her presentation?

answers.A: Bipolar II disorder, current depressive episode
answers.B: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
answers.C: Major depressive disorder with atypical features

explanations.A: No hypomanic episode is described, and the laboratory abnormality provides a direct physiologic explanation.
explanations.B: Overt primary hypothyroidism with a markedly elevated TSH and low free T4 is a recognized medical cause of depression, and correcting the thyroid disorder is the first treatment step.
explanations.C: Atypical MDD would be diagnosed only after excluding a medical cause, and here the thyroid studies establish one.
explanations.D: PDD requires at least 2 years of depressed mood; her symptoms have lasted 4 months.
explanations.E: No substance or medication exposure is described to account for the mood change.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with major depressive disorder has achieved full remission on sertraline over 4 months. He now reports delayed ejaculation and anorgasmia that he finds intolerable and is threatening to stop all treatment. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, and normal blood pressure. He wishes to switch to an agent that is unlikely to reproduce this adverse effect. Which drug is the most appropriate substitution?

explanations.A: Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake without meaningful serotonergic activity, so it lacks the serotonergically mediated sexual dysfunction seen with SSRIs and SNRIs.
explanations.B: Citalopram is another SSRI and would be expected to cause the same sexual dysfunction.
explanations.C: Duloxetine inhibits SERT and NET and carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction plus GI upset.
explanations.D: Paroxetine is among the SSRIs most associated with sexual dysfunction and anticholinergic effects.
explanations.E: Venlafaxine inhibits serotonin reuptake at therapeutic doses and can also raise blood pressure.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of a medication prescribed to her grandmother for depression and neuropathic pain. She is confused with dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, and absent bowel sounds. She then has a generalized seizure. Vital signs and ECG findings are shown. Which mechanism best explains the ECG abnormality?

answers.B: Blockade of peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
answers.C: Inhibition of cardiac fast sodium channels
answers.D: Inhibition of monoamine oxidase A in the gut wall

explanations.A: 5-HT2A antagonism contributes to sedation with agents such as trazodone but does not widen the QRS complex.
explanations.B: Alpha-1 blockade explains her hypotension and reflex tachycardia but not the prolonged QRS duration.
explanations.C: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac fast sodium channels, slowing phase 0 depolarization and widening the QRS, the finding that predicts ventricular arrhythmia and drives sodium bicarbonate therapy.
explanations.D: MAO inhibition in the gut underlies tyramine-mediated hypertensive crisis with MAOIs, not sodium channel blockade.
explanations.E: Antimuscarinic activity accounts for her dry skin, mydriasis, ileus, and tachycardia but does not affect QRS duration.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression presents with a severe occipital headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis 45 minutes after a dinner of aged cheddar, cured sausage, and red wine. He was started on a new antidepressant 3 weeks ago after failing two SSRIs. Vital signs are shown. Which medication is he most likely taking?

explanations.A: Amitriptyline causes anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiotoxicity rather than tyramine-triggered hypertension.
explanations.B: Bupropion can cause agitation, insomnia, and seizures but does not produce a food-triggered hypertensive crisis.
explanations.C: Mirtazapine causes sedation and weight gain through H1 and alpha-2 antagonism.
explanations.D: Phenelzine nonselectively inhibits monoamine oxidase, so dietary tyramine escapes gut and hepatic metabolism, displaces stored norepinephrine, and produces a hypertensive crisis.
explanations.E: Trazodone blocks H1, alpha-1, and 5-HT2 receptors, causing sedation, orthostasis, and priapism.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man with major depressive disorder and chronic insomnia was started on a new antidepressant 5 days ago to target both problems. He presents to the emergency department with a painful erection that has persisted for 4 hours and is unrelated to sexual activity. He takes no other medications and denies intracavernosal injections or sickle cell disease. Which medication is most likely responsible?

explanations.A: Bupropion is activating and typically worsens rather than treats insomnia, and it is not linked to priapism.
explanations.B: Fluoxetine causes sexual dysfunction in the form of delayed orgasm and reduced libido, not sustained erection.
explanations.C: Phenelzine carries risk of hypertensive crisis with tyramine and serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
explanations.D: Sertraline may cause GI upset and anorgasmia but is not associated with priapism.
explanations.E: Trazodone, a serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor with potent alpha-1 blockade, is commonly used for depression with insomnia and is the classic cause of drug-induced priapism.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder has been mute and immobile for 6 days, holding postures when her limbs are repositioned. She has refused all food and fluids for 4 days, states through written notes that she deserves to die, and believes her organs have rotted away. She has failed adequate trials of two antidepressants. Which treatment is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Bright-light therapy has its strongest evidence in seasonal depression and works far too slowly for a patient who is not eating.
explanations.B: Psychotherapy requires participation and engagement, which catatonia and psychosis preclude, and it acts too slowly here.
explanations.C: ECT is the most effective and fastest-acting treatment and is specifically indicated for severe depression with catatonia, psychotic features, food refusal, or imminent suicide risk.
explanations.D: rTMS is an option for treatment-resistant depression when a noninvasive outpatient approach is acceptable, but it is less rapid and less robust than ECT in a medical emergency.
explanations.E: VNS is reserved for chronic highly treatment-resistant depression after multiple failed treatments and provides only gradual, modest benefit.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man has major depressive disorder that has failed adequate trials of an SSRI, an SNRI, and augmentation with bupropion. He has no psychotic features, no catatonia, and no suicidal ideation, and he is eating and working. He declines electroconvulsive therapy because he cannot accept general anesthesia or the risk of memory effects, but he is willing to attend outpatient visits several times weekly for weeks. Which treatment is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Bright-light therapy is indicated primarily for seasonal depression and is an adjunct rather than a treatment-resistance strategy.
explanations.B: ECT is the most effective option but the patient has explicitly declined anesthesia and its cognitive effects.
explanations.C: Psychotherapy alone is first-line for mild depression and would be insufficient after three failed pharmacologic trials.
explanations.D: rTMS is a noninvasive outpatient neuromodulation option for treatment-resistant depression that requires no anesthesia, at the cost of frequent visits over several weeks.
explanations.E: VNS requires surgical implantation and is reserved for chronic, highly refractory illness after multiple failed treatments including neuromodulation.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is seen for a first psychiatric evaluation for 6 weeks of depressed mood and insomnia. While describing her symptoms she says, "Some mornings I wish I just wouldn't wake up." She has not previously disclosed this. The remainder of the history so far includes symptom onset, stressors, and effects on sleep and appetite. Which is the most appropriate next step in the interview?

answers.A: Ask about specific plan, intent, and access to means
answers.B: Complete a detailed birth and developmental history
answers.C: Document her religious and spiritual practices
answers.D: Obtain a full account of her legal problems
answers.E: Review family history of major medical illness

explanations.A: Any expression of suicidal ideation must be immediately characterized for plan, intent, and access to means, since this determines acute risk and disposition.
explanations.B: Developmental history is a standard component of the psychiatric history but is emphasized in pediatric patients and is not urgent here.
explanations.C: Religion and spirituality belong to the social history and can be explored after acute safety is established.
explanations.D: Legal history is part of the social history and does not take precedence over risk assessment.
explanations.E: Family history of medical illness is relevant background but does not address the immediate safety concern.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man is seen 6 months after an anterior myocardial infarction. He has stopped attending cardiac rehabilitation, has anhedonia and early morning awakening, and reports that his statin and beta-blocker bottles are still nearly full. Registry data indicate that his mood disorder roughly doubles his post-infarction mortality independently of adherence. Which physiologic mechanism best explains that independent excess risk?

answers.C: Increased heart rate variability from vagal tone
answers.D: Increased HPA axis activity with elevated cortisol
answers.E: Reduced circulating interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein

explanations.A: Depression increases platelet reactivity and aggregation, promoting thrombus formation; decreased aggregation would be protective.
explanations.B: Depression reduces nitric oxide bioavailability through inflammation and oxidative stress, causing vasoconstriction and accelerated atherosclerosis.
explanations.C: Depression is associated with reduced heart rate variability, reflecting sympathetic predominance and arrhythmia risk.
explanations.D: Depression activates the CRH-ACTH-cortisol axis, and the resulting hypercortisolemia drives central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and endothelial dysfunction independent of behavior.
explanations.E: Depression raises IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CRP; falling inflammatory markers would predict lower rather than higher cardiac risk.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes previously maintained excellent glycemic control. Over the past 8 months she has developed anhedonia, fatigue, and hopelessness, has stopped checking her glucose, and has missed two endocrinology visits. Her metformin dose is unchanged. Laboratory values from 1 year ago and today are shown. Which best explains the change?

answers.A: Decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis from cortisol deficiency
answers.B: Improved medication adherence with fewer refill gaps
answers.C: Increased insulin sensitivity from sympathetic withdrawal
answers.D: Reduced adherence plus cortisol-driven insulin resistance
answers.E: Suppression of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor

explanations.A: Her cortisol is elevated, not deficient, and hypercortisolemia increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose output.
explanations.B: The history documents worse self-management and missed visits, and improved adherence would lower rather than raise her A1c.
explanations.C: Depression produces sympathetic activation with decreased insulin sensitivity and increased glycogenolysis.
explanations.D: Depression worsens glycemic control through both behavioral pathways (nonadherence, reduced monitoring, poor diet) and physiologic pathways, chiefly HPA activation with hypercortisolemia and cytokine-impaired insulin signaling.
explanations.E: Her hs-CRP has risen, consistent with the inflammatory state of depression that impairs insulin signaling.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is evaluated 3 days after a motorcycle crash in which he sustained a proximal fibular fracture treated with a well-fitting cast. He cannot dorsiflex or evert the right foot and has a steppage gait. Inversion and plantarflexion are full strength, and hip abduction is normal. Sensation is decreased over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. The Achilles reflex is 2+ and symmetric. Which structure is injured?

explanations.A: The common fibular nerve wraps the fibular neck and supplies both its superficial branch (eversion, dorsum of foot sensation) and deep branch (dorsiflexion), so weak eversion plus weak dorsiflexion with a preserved ankle jerk localizes here.
explanations.B: Isolated deep fibular injury spares eversion and produces sensory loss confined to the first dorsal web space.
explanations.C: An L5 radiculopathy also weakens inversion (tibialis posterior) and hip abduction (gluteus medius), both of which are normal.
explanations.D: A sciatic lesion would additionally weaken plantarflexion and abolish the Achilles reflex.
explanations.E: Tibial nerve injury impairs plantarflexion, inversion, and toe flexion with loss of the ankle jerk and sole sensation.

questions.question: A 44-year-old warehouse worker reports 3 weeks of shooting pain from the buttock to the foot and a slapping gait. Examination shows weak dorsiflexion and weak great toe extension, weak foot inversion, and weak hip abduction with a positive Trendelenburg sign on that side. Plantarflexion is intact and the Achilles reflex is preserved. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Which structure is affected?

explanations.A: A common fibular lesion spares inversion and hip abduction, since tibialis posterior and gluteus medius are supplied by other nerves.
explanations.B: The deep fibular nerve supplies dorsiflexion and toe extension only, with web-space sensory loss and no proximal weakness.
explanations.C: Weak inversion (tibialis posterior) and weak hip abduction (gluteus medius) alongside foot drop indicate the deficit follows the L5 myotome rather than a single peripheral nerve, and radicular pain supports a root lesion.
explanations.D: S1 lesions weaken plantarflexion and abolish the Achilles reflex, both preserved here.
explanations.E: The superficial fibular nerve mediates eversion and dorsal foot sensation but not dorsiflexion, inversion, or hip abduction.

questions.question: A 28-year-old hiker reports 2 weeks of tripping over her toes after several days of wearing tightly laced stiff boots. She has weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension. Foot eversion is 5/5, plantarflexion is 5/5, and reflexes are normal and symmetric. The only sensory abnormality is decreased pinprick in the web space between the first and second toes. Which nerve is injured?

explanations.A: A common fibular lesion would also weaken eversion and cause broader sensory loss over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
explanations.B: The deep fibular nerve supplies tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus, and its only cutaneous territory is the first dorsal web space, which is the classic pattern of anterior compartment compression.
explanations.C: The saphenous nerve is purely sensory to the medial leg, ankle, and foot and carries no motor fibers.
explanations.D: The superficial fibular nerve produces weak eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot sparing the first web space.
explanations.E: The sural nerve is purely sensory to the lateral foot and posterolateral leg.

questions.question: A 48-year-old obese man reports 2 months of burning, tingling discomfort over the outer aspect of the right thigh from the hip toward the knee, worse when he wears a heavy tool belt and stands for long periods. Strength is 5/5 throughout the lower limbs including hip flexion and knee extension. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. There is no back pain and no bowel or bladder change. Which nerve is involved?

explanations.A: Femoral neuropathy would weaken knee extension and depress the patellar reflex, with numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg.
explanations.B: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and skin over the femoral triangle and is typically injured during inguinal surgery.
explanations.C: The iliohypogastric nerve supplies suprapubic skin and lower abdominal wall muscle and is injured during hernia repair or low abdominal incisions.
explanations.D: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-L3) is purely sensory to the lateral thigh; entrapment under the inguinal ligament produces meralgia paresthetica with burning pain and no weakness or reflex change.
explanations.E: Obturator neuropathy causes weak thigh adduction with medial thigh numbness, usually after pelvic surgery or labor.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman received an intramuscular injection into the buttock 1 week ago. She now has a waddling gait. When she stands on the affected leg, the opposite side of her pelvis drops. Hip extension, knee flexion, ankle plantarflexion, and dorsiflexion are all 5/5. Sensation is intact throughout the limb and all reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. Which nerve was injured?

explanations.A: Femoral injury weakens knee extension and reduces the patellar reflex with anterior thigh sensory loss.
explanations.B: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, so injury impairs rising from a chair, stair climbing, and running rather than pelvic stabilization.
explanations.C: Obturator injury weakens adduction and produces a wide, circumducting gait with medial thigh numbness.
explanations.D: Sciatic injury from a misplaced gluteal injection would cause weakness below the knee and sensory loss, both absent here.
explanations.E: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, which stabilize the pelvis in single-leg stance; injury produces a Trendelenburg sign with contralateral pelvic drop and no sensory deficit.

questions.question: A 41-year-old long-distance runner reports 3 months of burning pain and numbness on the sole of the right foot, worse at night and after running. Examination shows weak toe flexion and difficulty standing on tiptoe on the right. Percussion just posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus reproduces the paresthesias. Sensation over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg is normal. Which nerve is entrapped?

explanations.A: The common fibular nerve is compressed at the fibular neck, producing foot drop with lateral leg and dorsal foot numbness.
explanations.B: The deep fibular nerve mediates dorsiflexion with sensation limited to the first dorsal web space.
explanations.C: The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory femoral branch to the medial leg and ankle and does not innervate the sole.
explanations.D: The superficial fibular nerve mediates eversion and dorsal foot sensation, both normal here.
explanations.E: The tibial nerve passes through the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus and supplies the medial and lateral plantar nerves and intrinsic sole muscles, so entrapment causes plantar burning, weak toe flexion, and a positive Tinel sign there.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder is unable to form new memories after an episode of confusion and ophthalmoplegia. Autopsy in similar cases shows hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies. In the Papez circuit, hippocampal output travels through the fornix to the mammillary bodies. A lesion of which structure would interrupt the very next relay in this circuit?

explanations.A: The amygdala assigns emotional salience and mediates fear and threat detection; it is not a relay between the mammillary bodies and cingulate cortex.
explanations.B: The mammillothalamic tract carries mammillary body output to the anterior thalamic nuclei, which then project to the cingulate gyrus, making this the next relay in the Papez circuit.
explanations.C: The entorhinal cortex is the gateway for cortical input to and output from the hippocampus and lies at the end of the circuit, after the cingulate.
explanations.D: The hippocampus is the origin of the circuit and gives rise to the fornix, upstream of the mammillary bodies.
explanations.E: The cingulate gyrus receives input from the anterior thalamus and therefore lies one relay further downstream.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman undergoes sural nerve biopsy for an asymmetric painful neuropathy. Low-power microscopy shows the nerve divided into several rounded bundles of axons, each bundle circumscribed by a distinct sheet of flattened cells and dense connective tissue that forms a diffusion barrier around the bundle. Inflammatory infiltrate is concentrated at this barrier. Which structure is being described?

explanations.A: The endoneurium is loose connective tissue surrounding individual axons within a fascicle, not the boundary of the fascicle itself.
explanations.B: The epineurium is the outermost dense fibrous layer investing the entire nerve and carrying its blood vessels.
explanations.C: The myelin sheath is the spiral Schwann cell membrane wrapping a single axon and is not a connective tissue layer.
explanations.D: The perineurium is the layer of flattened cells and connective tissue that circumscribes each fascicle and forms the blood-nerve diffusion barrier.
explanations.E: The Schwann cell basal lamina surrounds individual Schwann cell-axon units and guides regeneration but does not define a fascicle.

questions.question: A 57-year-old woman treated with cisplatin develops profound loss of proprioception and vibration in all four limbs with sensory ataxia and pseudoathetosis. Strength is 5/5 everywhere and there is no muscle atrophy or fasciculation. Nerve conduction studies show absent sensory nerve action potentials with entirely normal compound muscle action potentials. Cell bodies in which location account for these findings?

answers.A: Anterior horn of the spinal cord
answers.B: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
answers.D: Lateral horn of the spinal cord

explanations.A: Anterior horn cells are the multipolar lower motor neurons; their loss causes weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations with reduced CMAPs.
explanations.B: Dorsal horn neurons are central second-order targets of primary afferents; their loss would not abolish peripherally recorded sensory nerve action potentials.
explanations.C: Primary sensory neurons are unipolar cells whose cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglion, a site outside the blood-nerve barrier that is selectively vulnerable to platinum agents, producing a pure sensory neuronopathy with absent SNAPs and normal CMAPs.
explanations.D: Lateral horn cells are preganglionic sympathetic neurons whose loss causes autonomic, not large-fiber sensory, failure.
explanations.E: Sympathetic chain ganglia contain postganglionic autonomic neurons that project to smooth muscle and glands.

questions.question: In a recording from a spinal motor neuron, a weak synaptic input produces a 4-mV depolarization that decays without spreading; a stronger input produces a 9-mV depolarization; a prolonged input produces a longer-lasting depolarization of the same peak amplitude. When several inputs arrive in rapid succession, an action potential of fixed amplitude is generated. Which statement best explains the firing?

answers.A: Graded potentials are all-or-none and arise at nodes of Ranvier
answers.B: Hyperpolarizing potentials propagate along the axon unchanged
answers.C: Larger stimuli generate proportionally larger action potentials
answers.D: Longer stimuli generate proportionally larger action potentials
answers.E: Summation of graded potentials at the axon hillock reaches threshold

explanations.A: Graded potentials are variable in amplitude and decremental; the all-or-none property belongs to the action potential.
explanations.B: Hyperpolarizing graded potentials, like depolarizing ones, decay with distance and do not propagate.
explanations.C: Once threshold is crossed the action potential amplitude is fixed; a larger stimulus increases firing frequency, not spike size.
explanations.D: A longer stimulus produces a longer-lasting graded depolarization but no increase in action potential amplitude, exactly as described.
explanations.E: EPSPs and IPSPs sum spatially and temporally at the axon hillock, and when the summed potential reaches threshold an all-or-none action potential is generated.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman reports 8 months of burning, tingling pain in both feet that is worse at night. Examination shows reduced pinprick and temperature sensation over the feet, normal vibration sense at the great toes, normal proprioception, 5/5 strength, and 2+ symmetric ankle reflexes. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography are entirely normal. Dysfunction of which fiber population best explains her findings?

answers.D: Small A-delta and unmyelinated C fibers
answers.E: Somatic motor fibers to skeletal muscle

explanations.A: A-alpha fibers carry proprioception and motor output; their loss would cause weakness, areflexia, and abnormal nerve conduction studies.
explanations.B: A-beta fibers mediate vibration and light touch, both preserved here, and their dysfunction would abnormalize conduction studies.
explanations.C: B fibers are preganglionic autonomic axons and do not mediate cutaneous pain and temperature sensation.
explanations.D: Pain and temperature travel in thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibers, which are too small to be assessed by conventional electrodiagnostics, so a small fiber neuropathy presents with burning pain and normal NCS/EMG.
explanations.E: Motor fiber involvement would produce weakness and abnormal compound muscle action potentials.

questions.question: The 54-year-old woman described above continues to have distal burning pain with preserved strength, vibration, and reflexes. Fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1c, vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid, thyroid studies, ESR, and serum immunofixation electrophoresis are all normal, and repeat nerve conduction studies and electromyography remain normal. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

answers.B: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
answers.C: MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast
answers.D: Repeat nerve conduction studies in 6 months
answers.E: Skin punch biopsy of the distal lower leg

explanations.A: EMG assesses denervation and reinnervation in large motor fibers and will remain normal in a pure small fiber process.
explanations.B: CSF analysis is used to look for albuminocytologic dissociation in acquired demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathies, which this indolent painful syndrome is not.
explanations.C: Lumbosacral MRI evaluates root compression and would not detect small fiber pathology in a patient without radicular features.
explanations.D: Repeating a test that only interrogates large myelinated fibers will not establish the diagnosis regardless of interval.
explanations.E: A 3-mm skin punch biopsy with PGP 9.5 immunostaining quantifies intraepidermal nerve fiber density, and a reduced density confirms small fiber neuropathy when NCS and EMG are normal.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man who had a partial gastrectomy 8 years ago reports 6 months of numb, clumsy hands and unsteady walking. Examination shows loss of vibration and proprioception at the toes and fingers, a positive Romberg sign, and brisk knee reflexes with an extensor plantar response. He follows a restricted diet and takes no supplements. Laboratory studies are shown. Which is the most likely cause?

explanations.A: Alcohol-related neuropathy is a painful distal sensorimotor axonal process and does not cause macrocytic anemia with elevated methylmalonic acid or upper motor neuron signs.
explanations.B: Charcot-Marie-Tooth is hereditary, begins in youth with foot deformities and distal atrophy, and does not produce anemia.
explanations.C: His hemoglobin A1c is normal, excluding diabetes as the driver of a length-dependent neuropathy.
explanations.D: Post-gastrectomy malabsorption with a low B12 and markedly elevated methylmalonic acid explains macrocytic anemia plus combined dorsal column and corticospinal involvement (subacute combined degeneration).
explanations.E: Pyridoxine deficiency causes seizures, glossitis, scaly dermatitis, and sideroblastic anemia rather than macrocytosis with elevated methylmalonic acid.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man reports lifelong difficulty running and frequent ankle sprains, worsening over several years. Examination shows bilateral pes cavus, hammer toes, distal leg atrophy with an inverted champagne bottle appearance, symmetric distal weakness, and absent ankle reflexes. His father and paternal aunt have similar feet. Nerve conduction studies show uniformly slowed conduction velocities in all limbs. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanations.A: An autosomal dominant family history with pes cavus, hammer toes, distal atrophy, and uniform conduction slowing is characteristic of hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth).
explanations.B: CIDP is an acquired relapsing or progressive demyelinating neuropathy with proximal and distal weakness, non-uniform conduction slowing, and albuminocytologic dissociation; it does not cause lifelong foot deformities or a family history.
explanations.C: Diabetic polyneuropathy is an acquired length-dependent axonal, sensory-predominant process in a patient with hyperglycemia.
explanations.D: GBS evolves over days to 4 weeks with ascending weakness and areflexia after an infection, not over years.
explanations.E: Vasculitic neuropathy is asymmetric and subacute with systemic features such as weight loss, rash, and elevated inflammatory markers.

questions.question: A 59-year-old woman reports that over 6 weeks she developed a right foot drop, then 2 weeks later a left ulnar sensory deficit and weak finger abduction. She has lost 7 kg, has a purpuric rash on the lower legs, and has microscopic hematuria. ESR is 92 mm/h and ANCA is positive. Nerve conduction studies show asymmetric axonal loss in individually affected nerves. Which etiology best explains her neuropathy?

explanations.A: Charcot-Marie-Tooth is symmetric, hereditary, and slowly progressive without systemic inflammatory features.
explanations.B: CIDP produces symmetric proximal and distal weakness with demyelinating conduction changes rather than stepwise asymmetric axonal deficits.
explanations.C: Diabetic polyneuropathy is symmetric and length dependent, beginning in the toes rather than in individual named nerves.
explanations.D: Thiamine deficiency causes a distal symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy, often with ataxia, confusion, and abnormal eye movements.
explanations.E: Sequential involvement of individual named nerves (mononeuritis multiplex) with weight loss, palpable purpura, hematuria, elevated ESR, and positive ANCA indicates ischemic nerve infarction from systemic vasculitis.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman has 6 weeks of progressive proximal and distal limb weakness with generalized areflexia and only mild distal numbness. Electrodiagnostic study results from the right leg are shown. Which interpretation of these findings is most accurate?

answers.A: Axonal neuropathy with early sensory involvement
answers.C: Myopathy with early recruitment on exertion

explanations.A: Axonal neuropathy reduces SNAP amplitudes first and then CMAP amplitudes, with conduction velocity relatively preserved; her distal amplitudes and SNAP are normal.
explanations.B: Markedly slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latency, and a large drop in CMAP amplitude between proximal and distal stimulation (conduction block) with preserved distal amplitudes define a demyelinating process.
explanations.C: Myopathy is diagnosed on needle EMG by low-amplitude short-duration polyphasic units with early recruitment, not by slowed nerve conduction.
explanations.D: Neuromuscular junction disorders are identified with repetitive stimulation showing decrement or increment, with normal conduction velocities and latencies.
explanations.E: Small fiber neuropathy leaves conventional nerve conduction studies normal, since they assess only large myelinated fibers.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man has 5 days of progressive leg weakness that began in the feet and has ascended to the thighs, and he now cannot climb stairs. Three weeks ago he had 4 days of bloody diarrhea after a barbecue. Examination shows symmetric flaccid weakness, absent deep tendon reflexes in all four limbs, mild distal paresthesias, and bilateral facial weakness. Lumbar puncture results are shown. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanations.A: Ascending symmetric flaccid weakness with areflexia and facial diplegia weeks after a diarrheal illness, plus albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cell count), is classic AIDP.
explanations.B: Botulism causes descending paralysis with prominent bulbar onset, fixed dilated pupils, and normal CSF protein.
explanations.C: Myasthenia gravis produces fatigable ptosis and diplopia with preserved reflexes and normal CSF.
explanations.D: Tick paralysis causes rapid ascending weakness but resolves after tick removal and does not raise CSF protein.
explanations.E: Transverse myelitis produces a sensory level with bowel and bladder involvement and, after spinal shock, upper motor neuron signs.

questions.question: The 27-year-old man described above reports that his diarrheal illness followed a meal of undercooked chicken and that several picnic attendees had similar symptoms. Stool culture from that illness was incubated at 42 C under microaerophilic conditions and grew an oxidase-positive, comma-shaped gram-negative rod. Which organism most likely triggered his neurologic illness?

explanations.A: A curved, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that grows microaerophilically at 42 C after undercooked poultry exposure is Campylobacter jejuni, the most common antecedent infection in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
explanations.B: CMV is an enveloped double-stranded DNA beta-herpesvirus that precedes GBS after a mononucleosis-like illness, not a bloody diarrheal illness, and would not grow on stool culture.
explanations.C: EBV is an enveloped double-stranded DNA gamma-herpesvirus causing pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis.
explanations.D: Influenza A is an enveloped, segmented, negative-sense ssRNA orthomyxovirus that causes a respiratory prodrome.
explanations.E: Salmonella is a gram-negative rod causing diarrheal illness but is not curved, does not require 42 C microaerophilic growth, and is not the classic GBS trigger.

questions.question: Sural nerve biopsy in a patient with ascending weakness after a Campylobacter jejuni infection shows macrophages stripping myelin lamellae from Schwann cells at the nodes of Ranvier, with complement deposition and relative preservation of the underlying axons. Serum contains IgG antibodies reactive with GM1. Which mechanism best explains how the preceding infection produced these findings?

answers.A: Antigen-independent superantigen activation of T cells
answers.B: Cross-reactive antibodies bind peripheral nerve gangliosides
answers.C: Direct invasion of Schwann cells by replicating bacteria
answers.D: Immune complex deposition within endoneurial blood vessels
answers.E: Toxin-mediated blockade of presynaptic acetylcholine release

explanations.A: Superantigens crosslink MHC II and T-cell receptors to cause massive nonspecific cytokine release, which does not generate antiganglioside IgG.
explanations.B: C. jejuni lipooligosaccharide carries carbohydrate epitopes nearly identical to peripheral nerve gangliosides such as GM1, so the IgG raised against the organism cross-reacts with myelin, fixes complement, and recruits macrophages that strip myelin (molecular mimicry).
explanations.C: C. jejuni does not invade or replicate within Schwann cells; the nerve injury is immune-mediated and occurs after the enteric infection has cleared.
explanations.D: Immune complex vasculitis produces ischemic axonal infarction in a mononeuritis multiplex pattern rather than complement-mediated segmental demyelination.
explanations.E: Presynaptic acetylcholine release blockade is the mechanism of botulinum toxin, which spares myelin entirely.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman admitted 2 days ago with Guillain-Barre syndrome now cannot lift her arms off the bed and speaks in short broken phrases. She is anxious and using accessory muscles. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air and a chest radiograph is clear. Bedside respiratory measurements over the last 12 hours are shown (weight 70 kg). Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.C: Obtain MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast
answers.D: Repeat lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis
answers.E: Start high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy

explanations.A: Corticosteroids are ineffective in AIDP and may worsen outcomes; they do not address impending respiratory failure.
explanations.B: A falling FVC below 15-20 mL/kg with a negative inspiratory force less negative than -30 cm H2O and a rising PaCO2 indicates neuromuscular respiratory failure, and elective intubation before decompensation is the standard response.
explanations.C: MRI is used to exclude mimics such as transverse myelitis and has no role once the diagnosis is established and the airway is threatened.
explanations.D: Repeating the lumbar puncture adds nothing to management and delays airway protection.
explanations.E: Oxygenation is preserved; the problem is ventilatory pump failure, which supplemental oxygen cannot correct and which may mask rising PaCO2.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with Guillain-Barre syndrome has progressed over 8 days and can no longer walk 10 meters unaided. He has labile blood pressure and mild dysphagia but an adequate forced vital capacity. Symptom onset was 10 days ago. He has no IgA deficiency, no renal impairment, and no thrombotic risk factors, and central venous access has not been established. Which treatment is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Corticosteroids have no benefit in AIDP and may exacerbate the course, unlike in CIDP.
explanations.B: Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and has no role in an antibody-mediated demyelinating neuropathy.
explanations.C: Inability to walk 10 meters unaided within 4 weeks of onset is a standard indication for immunotherapy, and IVIG is as effective as plasma exchange while requiring no central line, making it preferred here.
explanations.D: Gabapentin and rehabilitation address neuropathic pain and recovery but do not modify the immune attack in a patient who is still progressing.
explanations.E: Interferon beta is a disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, a central demyelinating disease.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman with AIDP cannot walk unaided and is being planned for immunotherapy. Her history includes recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and prior workup documented selective IgA deficiency with detectable anti-IgA antibodies. She had an anaphylactic reaction to a blood product 5 years ago. Renal function is normal and she has good peripheral and central venous access. Which treatment is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Corticosteroids are ineffective in AIDP and could exacerbate symptoms.
explanations.B: IVIG is contraindicated here because anti-IgA antibodies in an IgA-deficient patient predispose to anaphylaxis with immunoglobulin preparations.
explanations.C: Azathioprine acts over months and has no role in acute AIDP.
explanations.D: An oral steroid taper likewise lacks efficacy in AIDP regardless of route or dose.
explanations.E: Plasma exchange removes pathogenic autoantibodies, complement, and immune complexes, is as effective as IVIG, and avoids the anti-IgA anaphylaxis risk; its main risks are hypotension, hypocalcemia, bleeding, and line complications.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man intubated for AIDP has had a femoral central venous catheter in place for 11 days, retained only for convenience of blood draws since vasopressors were stopped on day 3. He now has a fever of 39.1 C, and two peripheral blood cultures and a catheter-drawn culture grow coagulase-negative staphylococci. Which measure would most likely have prevented this infection?

answers.C: Prompt removal of the catheter once nonessential
answers.D: Routine guidewire exchange of the catheter every 72 hours
answers.E: Shaving the insertion site with a razor before draping

explanations.A: Systemic antibiotic prophylaxis at insertion is not recommended, does not prevent CLABSI, and promotes resistance and C. difficile infection.
explanations.B: Chlorhexidine 2% is the recommended skin antiseptic and outperforms povidone-iodine, so this substitution would increase risk.
explanations.C: Daily review with prompt removal of a catheter that is no longer essential is a core CLABSI prevention bundle element, and infection risk rises with each additional catheter day; the line here had been unnecessary for over a week.
explanations.D: Scheduled guidewire exchanges do not reduce infection and add mechanical complication risk.
explanations.E: Razor shaving causes microabrasions that increase infection risk; clippers are preferred when hair removal is necessary.
